options: It runs the command's action whenever the bound button is clicked
It notifies the UI to re-evaluate whether the command is enabled
It returns `true` or `false` to enable or disable the button
It passes the `CommandParameter` to `Execute`
questions.explanation: `CanExecute` controls whether the command is enabled, `Execute` runs when it is invoked, and the `CanExecuteChanged` event notifies the UI to re-evaluate the enabled state.

questions.prompt: The ViewModel creates `IncrementCommand = new RelayCommand(Increment);` with no `canExecute` delegate. Using the classic RelayCommand, what does `CanExecute` return?
options: It throws an `ArgumentNullException`
`false`, so the button starts disabled
`true`, through the `?? true` fallback
Whatever value `Increment()` returns
questions.explanation: `canExecute` defaults to `null`, and `CanExecute` is `_canExecute?.Invoke() ?? true`, so a command without a predicate is always executable. Only a null `execute` throws.

questions.prompt: `DeleteSelectedCommand` can execute only when `SelectedTransaction != null`. Why does the property setter call `CommandManager.InvalidateRequerySuggested()`?
options: No input event occurs, so WPF would not re-check `CanExecute`
It deletes the selected transaction from the list right away
It is required for `OnPropertyChanged()` to notify the UI
It stops WPF from calling `CanExecute` more often than needed
questions.explanation: CommandManager re-evaluates commands after events like focus changes and mouse clicks. When only the selection changes, WPF does not know something changed, so `InvalidateRequerySuggested()` forces it to re-check all commands now.

questions.prompt: Put what happens after a ViewModel calls `CommandManager.InvalidateRequerySuggested()` in order.
steps: The button enables or disables itself
questions.explanation: RelayCommand's `CanExecuteChanged` is wired to `CommandManager.RequerySuggested`, so raising it makes each bound button call `CanExecute()` and update its enabled state.

questions.prompt: Which of these does **not** make CommandManager re-check `CanExecute()` automatically?
options: Keyboard focus changing
A mouse click
The window activating or deactivating
A ViewModel property being set from code
questions.explanation: WPF re-checks commands on keyboard focus changes, mouse clicks, window activation/deactivation and menus opening. A property set in code produces none of these, which is why you invalidate or raise `CanExecuteChanged` yourself.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson recommend a RelayCommand that raises `CanExecuteChanged` manually (`DeleteCommand.RaiseCanExecuteChanged()`) over relying on CommandManager?
options: Manual raising refreshes every command in the whole app at once
It is a local, explicit refresh that is async-friendly and testable
CommandManager cannot be used together with `ObservableCollection`
Manual raising lets the button skip calling `CanExecute` entirely
questions.explanation: CommandManager does a global, implicit refresh that is not async-friendly and is hard to test. The manual approach is explicit and local, async-friendly, easy to test and highly predictable.
